<noinclude><pagequality level="3" user="BRPXQZME" />{{running header|390|{{asc|THE SHIH KING.}}|{{smaller|{{asc|DECADE I.}}}}}}{{rule}}</noinclude>state, raised up a proper ruler<ref name="p390_1">[[w:King Wen of Zhou|King Wăn]] is 'the proper ruler' intended here, and the next line intimates that this was determined before there was any likelihood of his becoming the ruler even of the [[w:Predynastic Zhou|territory of ''K''âu]];—another instance of the foreseeing providence ascribed to God. [[w:Taibo|Thâi-po]] was the eldest son of [[w:King Tai of Zhou|king Thâi]], and [[w:Ji, King of Zhou|king ''K''î]] was, perhaps, only the third. The succession ought to have come to Thâi-po; but he, seeing the sage virtues of {{tooltip|''Kh''ang|Chāng}} (afterwards king Wăn), the son of ''K''î, and seeing also that king Thâi was anxious that this boy should ultimately become ruler of ''K''âu, voluntarily withdrew from ''K''âu altogether, and left the state to ''K''î and his son. See the remark of [[Author:Confucius|Confucius]] on Thâi-po's conduct, in the [[Analects]], VIII, i.</ref> for it,—{{lb}}From
the time of {{tooltip|Thâi-po|Tàibó}} and king {{tooltip|''K''î|Jì}} (this was done)<ref name="p390_1" />.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Now this king ''K''î{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
In his heart was full of brotherly duty.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Full of duty to his elder brother,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
He gave himself the more to promote the prosperity (of the country),{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
And secured to him the glory (of his act)<ref>The lines from six to ten speak of [[w:Ji, King of Zhou|king ''K''î]] in his relation to his elder brother. He accepted [[w:Taibo|Thâi-po]]'s act without any failure of his own duty to him, and by his own improvement of it, made his brother more glorious through it. His feeling of brotherly duty was simply the natural instinct of his heart. Having accepted the act, it only made him the more anxious to promote the good of the state, and thus he made his brother more glorious by showing what advantages accrued from his resignation and withdrawal from [[w:Predynastic Zhou|''K''âu]].</ref>.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
He accepted his dignity and did not lose it,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
And (ere long his family) possessed the whole kingdom.

This king ''K''î{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Was gifted by God with the power of judgment,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
So that the fame of his virtue silently grew.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
His virtue was highly intelligent,—{{lb}}Highly
intelligent, and of rare discrimination;{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Able to lead, able to rule,{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
To rule over this great country;{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
Rendering a cordial submission, effecting a cordial union<ref name="p390_3">This line refers to [[w:Ji, King of Zhou|''K''î]]'s maintenance of his own loyal duty</ref>.{{page other|{{wsp|0.5em}}|{{br}}}}
